Experiments that changed questions

The "Eat at Joe's" sign: we think others think like us

Walking around campus wearing a silly sign. How many would agree? It depends on what you decided.

In 1977, Lee Ross and colleagues at Stanford asked students whether they would walk around campus for half an hour wearing a sign that said "Eat at Joe's". Then they asked them to estimate how many fellow students would agree.

False consensus

Those who agreed thought most others would too; those who refused thought most would refuse. Each group believed its choice was the more common one and that the opposite choice said something about the person's character.

They called it the false consensus effect. It shows up in political views, tastes and habits, and is reinforced because we tend to surround ourselves with similar people. Remembering it helps us be less surprised when others decide differently.

References

  1. Ross, L., Greene, D. y House, P. (1977). The "false consensus effect". Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 13(3), 279–301.
